subsystems.name: Telescope and optics
subsystems.role: collects enough starlight to spread across many wavelengths at once.

subsystems.name: Spectrograph
subsystems.role: separates the light into a spectrum fine enough to resolve narrow absorption bands.
parts: dispersion element such as a grating or prism

subsystems.name: Calibration and stability
subsystems.role: holds the instrument's wavelength scale and response steady while the star is observed.
parts: reference lamps or laser frequency combs

subsystems.name: Data reduction pipeline
subsystems.role: turns raw detector frames into calibrated spectra and removes instrument systematics.

subsystems.name: Atmospheric retrieval
subsystems.role: interprets measured transit depths as molecules, clouds and temperature structure.

buildSteps.title: Choose a target and predict its transit
buildSteps.detail: Select a planet whose orbit crosses the face of its star as seen from Earth, and calculate when the crossing occurs and how long it lasts.

buildSteps.title: Design or configure the spectrograph
buildSteps.detail: Build an instrument that covers the needed visible or infrared bands, with a stable optical bench and a detector able to record the star and the planet's limb together.

buildSteps.title: Integrate with a telescope
buildSteps.detail: Mount the spectrograph on a space telescope or a large ground-based telescope, and verify that pointing drifts or atmospheric turbulence stay below the size of the signal sought.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the instrument
buildSteps.detail: Measure detector response, wavelength scale and throughput using reference sources, then track how they change over time.

buildSteps.title: Observe the transit
buildSteps.detail: Record spectra continuously before, during and after the planet crosses the star, so the out-of-transit data provides a baseline.

buildSteps.title: Reduce and correct the data
buildSteps.detail: Extract spectra, correct for detector and pointing systematics, and model stellar activity such as spots and faculae that can mimic an atmosphere.

buildSteps.title: Measure wavelength-dependent transit depths
buildSteps.detail: Compare in-transit and out-of-transit flux in each wavelength bin to find where the planet blocks a slightly larger fraction of the star's light.

buildSteps.title: Fit atmospheric models
buildSteps.detail: Use retrieval codes to test which molecules, clouds and hazes best explain the measured spectrum, and report confidence limits.

prerequisites.why: the atmospheric signal is a tiny change in the star's apparent size, far smaller than the star itself.
the instrument must record bright starlight and very small absorption features without saturating or adding noise.

prerequisites.tech: Space telescopes with coverage across key infrared bands
prerequisites.why: Earth's atmosphere absorbs many infrared wavelengths that carry important molecular signatures.
spots, faculae and plages can create signals larger than the planet's atmosphere.

prerequisites.tech: Complete molecular line lists and cloud models
prerequisites.why: some molecules and cloud properties are poorly known, limiting how confidently a detection can be interpreted.

pathway.milestone: JWST and Hubble are measuring transmission spectra of gas giants and some rocky planets
pathway.unlocks: detections of water, carbon dioxide and other molecules in exoplanet atmospheres.

pathway.milestone: dedicated exoplanet-atmosphere missions and extreme-precision ground spectrographs enlarge the sample
pathway.unlocks: comparative planetology: how atmospheres differ with planet size, temperature and host star.

pathway.milestone: combining transmission with emission and phase-curve measurements
pathway.unlocks: three-dimensional views of weather, heat transport and clouds.

pathway.milestone: searching habitable-zone rocky planets for biosignature gases
pathway.unlocks: candidate signs of life, though stellar contamination and false positives must first be ruled out.
